summary: Under the problem's explicit unit-cost concatenation model, one concatenation can at most double the available copy count, while binary doubling constructs exactly n copies in logarithmically many iterations.

optimality.argument: Starting from one copy, after k concatenations no constructed block can contain more than 2^k copies because one operation combines only two previously available strings. Reaching n copies therefore requires Omega(log n) concatenations in the stated model. The accepted algorithm halves n each iteration, doubles one block, and appends that block for set bits, establishing O(log n).

replacement_checks.evidence: A concatenation combines two existing repetition blocks, so the maximum constructible copy count grows by at most a factor of two per operation.
Binary decomposition processes one bit of n per loop iteration and performs at most two unit-cost concatenations for that bit.

Node regression covers the authored cases, powers of two, mixed set bits, receiver preservation, the maximum repetition count, and confirms the built-in repeat method is absent from the accepted source.
